research.topic: Agricultural inspection craft and visual-line-of-sight rules (2026)
bullets: Small uncrewed craft already fly inspection and spray routes over orchards and vineyards where a person on the ground can keep them in sight.
Beyond-line-of-sight work is still gated by local rules, radio, and a watcher — capability alone does not invent the packing-floor workflow.

grounding:
## Technology
- **emTech:** drones
- **Product category:** Low-altitude orchard inspection craft — cameras and simple sensors on a small airframe that can hug tree rows and return a same-morning map of hail, rot, and gaps.

## Capabilities
A trained operator can cover far blocks in one pass that would take a walker until noon, and mark fruit that is brown under the skin, provided battery, radio, and a legal watcher exist. Spray and delivery are a different product; this tile is look-and-map.

## Trends & predictions
Airframes got cheaper and more field-rugged through 2025–2026; software stitches a row into a picture a packing lead can read. **Forecast (not lock):** same-morning orchard maps become routine where county rules and a spare operator hold.

## Milestone
Around 2026, small inspection craft plus stitching software make a same-morning far-block read realistic for a family orchard — not only for a research station.

## Honest limits
Wind after hail grounds the craft. A county visual-line-of-sight rule still needs a watcher unless the invent changes how looking is done. No full agronomy team. Pilot one orchard, one morning, not a county fleet.

## Unlocks Use Case(s)
Same-morning hail and rot maps for packing decisions; a record a buyer can see that a walker cannot fake.

## Applications
Packing-shed flight runbooks; row-map boards the night crew can read; a watcher workflow that does not steal the whole floor — invent the local system.

mission.briefMd:
## The place

Elena tapes a hail tag on the first bin at **Peck Orchard**. Dawn. Willow Cut still smells like wet leaves. The buyer trucks come at ten. The near rows she can walk. Past the third block the trees close over, and last night's hail is a rumor.

She picks one apple from the near row. Sound. She picks one from the edge of the far block. Brown under the skin. She cannot walk every row before the trucks. Last year she guessed. The packing floor threw out two bins that were fine, and kept one that was not. The buyer cut the contract for a month.

The county clerk left a laminated card on the packing-shed door. Any craft that leaves the tree line needs a watcher who can see it the whole time. Elena has four people on the floor and none to spare on a hill. The far blocks stay a guess.

The pickers wait by the bins. If she sends them into spoiled fruit they lose the morning. If she holds them they miss the trucks. Either way the floor goes quiet.

## The bigger problem

This is how a harvest dies in the rows nobody can walk. Truth lives at walking speed. Hail, heat, and blight do not. A farm that only believes what a person can see before the buyer comes will throw good fruit and ship bad fruit in the same hour.

The root is not a missing pair of eyes in the sky. It is a packing floor that has no way to know the far blocks in the hour it still has, and a county rule that treats looking from above as a spectacle that needs a babysitter. Every orchard on this ridge lives under the same clock.

## Your job

Invent a way this packing floor can know which far-block fruit is still good before the trucks leave, without walking every row. Stakeholder: **Elena Ruiz, night packing lead**.
